title: Root-to-Leaf Path Sum
statement:
A pricing engine walks a decision tree. It starts at the root, and at each node it adds that node's adjustment to the price, then moves to one child, until it reaches a node with no children. Adjustments can be negative. QA asks: can any complete route produce a total of exactly target?

Trees use LeetCode's list format: tree[0] is the root, then the children of each node, left before right, level by level. None marks a missing child, and missing nodes list no children. Trailing Nones may be left off, and [] is the empty tree.

A leaf is a node with no children. A path must start at the root and end at a leaf; stopping at a node that still has a child does not count. The empty tree has no paths, so its answer is False, even for target = 0.

Write def solution(tree, target) that returns True if at least one root-to-leaf path has values that add up to exactly target, and False otherwise. Trees can be 10,000 levels deep, so avoid recursion.

examples.input: tree = [5, 4, 8, 11, None, 13, 4, 7, 2, None, None, None, 1], target = 22

examples.why: The two paths add up to 3 and 4. Neither is 5.
The empty tree has no root-to-leaf path at all.

constraints: the tree can be 10,000 levels deep

think.q: What exactly counts as a path, and what does not?
think.a: Only full routes: root to a leaf, a node with no left and no right child. In [1, 2] with target 1, the root alone sums to 1 but it has a child, so it is not a leaf and the answer is False.

Two leaves, so two paths: 1 + 2 = 3 and 1 + 3 = 4. Target 5 matches neither, so False. Notice that each sum is the parent's running sum plus the child's value: you never need the whole path, only the total so far.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Record every root-to-leaf path as a list of values, then sum each list. Copying the path at every node costs O(height) per node, so a deep tree takes O(n * h), which is O(n^2) on a chain.

Depth-first search carrying a running sum. Push (node, sum including node) on an explicit stack. When you pop a leaf, compare its sum with target. Otherwise push each child with sum + child.val. Values can be negative, so you cannot stop early when a sum passes the target.

1. Build the tree. If it is empty, return False.
  2. stack = [(root, root.val)].
  3. Pop (node, total). If node has no children and total == target, return True.
  4. Push each existing child with total + child.val.
  5. When the stack is empty, return False.

Empty tree with target = 0 (still False). A sum that matches at a node with one child (not a leaf). A single node equal to the target. Negative values, where a path can go above the target and come back. Zero values. A 10,000-deep tree, where recursion overflows.

hints: You never need the whole path, only its total so far. A child's total is its parent's total plus the child's value.
Use a stack of (node, total) pairs. Only check the target when the popped node has no children.
Do not prune when a total passes the target: a later negative value can bring it back. The empty tree returns False before anything else.
explain:
Example 1: the root 5 has children 4 and 8; 4 leads to 11, whose children are 7 and 2; 8 leads to 13 and 4, and that 4 has a right child 1. Target 22.

  • Start with (5, 5). Pop it and push (4, 9) and (8, 13).
  • Pop (8, 13): push (13, 26) and (4, 17). Pop (4, 17): push (1, 18). The leaves 1 (sum 18) and 13 (sum 26) do not match.
  • Pop (4, 9): push (11, 20). Pop it: push (7, 27) and (2, 22).
  • Pop (2, 22): a leaf with sum 22. Return True.

Each node is pushed and popped once, and each stack entry holds one number instead of a whole path, so the work is O(n). The stack holds at most about one entry per level plus the waiting siblings, so it grows with the height of the tree, not with recursion depth.
complexity: O(n) time, O(height) extra space for the stack
